Win probabilities corrected — one value across every page
rows.evidence: AUTO-HELD on its own gate 2026-08-11, closed with the reason and the number. Two of the three checks passed: after repointing, all four pins read one identical value, and the served probability reproduced twice - from the recorded measurement at 12.5569 on 1,474 games, and by recomputing every one of the 268 served rows from its own stored spread and centre with zero mismatches. THE FAILING NUMBER IS COVERAGE: 90.11 percent against a required 89 to 90, measured on 182 played regular-season games. It misses by eleven hundredths of a point and turns on a single game - 164 of 182 inside; 163 would have passed - and it errs wide, which is the safe direction. Nothing was tuned toward the bar: the spread is measured from residuals and the module states in its own header that the band is never widened to reach a coverage bar. The repoint was reverted, so the promote did not ship.

agent_updates.title: Why All-Star scoring exploded, and why it is not because the games got faster
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** All-Star scoring has roughly exploded over 27 years, and the obvious explanation - that the games keep getting faster - turns out to be wrong. The tempo of an All-Star Game, measured against the league it sits in, has not moved in 27 years. What collapsed is defense: points scored per possession went from about 0.85 to about 1.36.

**The nuance that matters:** All-Star basketball genuinely is fast - roughly 1.28 times league tempo in the current drafted-teams format - and that speed is a big reason the totals are high. But it has always been fast. The *rise* is entirely the disappearing defense, not an acceleration.

**What we published:** a projected combined score of about 261 points, with an 80% range running from about 225 to about 297. That range is wide on purpose. Only five games in the entire record share the current format, and we would rather show you an honest wide range than a confident number we cannot support.

**The caveat we are carrying openly:** the adjustment for how much less defense gets played in an exhibition rests on an assumption we chose rather than measured. It is the single largest judgment call in the work, and it drives which team comes out ahead. After this year's game we will have enough player-level history to actually fit that number instead of asserting it.

agent_updates.title: We were mispricing questionable players - in both directions at once
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** When a player was listed as probable, we treated that as a 95% chance she takes the floor. Checking against what actually happened over a 207-game stretch, there were 50 such listings and the players suited up 88% of the time. We were too optimistic.

**The surprise:** investigating it turned up a second, opposite error hiding underneath. Only about half of those listings were ever getting the 95% figure. The other half were being priced at 55% - against a real play rate of 92%. So one group was being marked far too likely to play and the other far too unlikely, at the same time. Both halves are now corrected.

**Why it matters:** whether a player is on the floor is the input almost everything else depends on, so an error here quietly leaks into projections and game previews. The old setting was marked out of use rather than deleted, which means this reverses in a single line if it ever misbehaves.

items.status: CLOSED 2026-08-12 AS ALREADY-TRUE. THE SQL IS AS DESCRIBED AND THE PUBLISHED NUMBERS ARE NOT SPLIT - THE ROW READ THE GROUP BY AND NOT THE OUTPUT. Both GROUP BY sites are exactly as filed: scripts/build_site.py line 3868 groups by player_id, player_name and line 5811 by player_id, player_name, season, team_abbr, both on . But the resolution happens DOWNSTREAM of the aggregate, before anything publishes. MEASURED ON THIS ROW'S OWN EXAMPLE. Jewell Loyd holds two identifiers in : 204319 with 371 games and 11207.3 minutes, and 2987869 with 31 games and 845.0 minutes. Entity total 402 games, 12052.3 minutes - and site/players.json serves career_min 12052.3, the FULL entity total, not a half. The row cites 402 games as the true figure, which is precisely the merged number already being served. THE PER-SEASON SURFACE IS ALSO WHOLE. site/compare_seasons.json carries Jewell Loyd ONCE, keyed on the name key jewell loyd, with all twelve seasons 2015 through 2026 present - and 2026 there is 31 games and 845.0 minutes, which is the SECOND identifier's data sitting beside the first identifier's 2015 to 2025. One node, both ids, no split. THE MECHANISM, so nobody re-files this. Immediately after the first aggregate, build_site.py:3871 builds a union-find over name and id pairs and unions each row's normalized name with its raw id, then sums games and minutes across every component of the entity. Its own comment records the 2026-07-30 extension that unioned SEASONS too, having measured 154 of 556 players under-reporting their season count. compare_seasons resolves through name keys instead, which is why it carries a complete career across an id migration. Keying the GROUP BY on the raw identifier is therefore not a defect on its own; it is an intermediate the resolver consumes. THE LESSON THIS ROW IS AN INSTANCE OF: reading the aggregate is not reading the published number. A two-word change to those GROUP BY clauses would have been made against a surface that was already correct, and on this repo's own evidence it could have regressed the union - the resolver keys on the raw id, so changing what the aggregate emits changes what the resolver has to work with. NOT LABELLED APPLY, deliberately: it is not finished-work-awaiting-wiring, it is finished.

data.status: open MEASURED 2026-08-12 AND THE ANSWER IS THAT THERE IS ONLY ONE WOMAN - THE FEARED MERGE IS NOT A MERGE OF TWO IDENTITIES. This row holds back a correct alias on the belief that declaring it would pool two women's records. It would not. Measured on : id 1628922, spelled Azura Stevens WITH the accent, carries 220 games across 2018 to 2025. id 3142010, spelled without it, carries 68 games across 2025 and 2026. FORTY-FOUR GAME IDS APPEAR UNDER BOTH, and on all 44 the game DATE, the TEAM, the POINTS, the REBOUNDS and the ASSISTS agree exactly - same date, same LAS, same box line. Two different women do not play the same 44 games under the same name with the same box score. It is one person recorded twice. A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FIRST CHECK, because it nearly sent me the other way. Comparing min, pts, reb and team_abbr together returned 0 of 44 identical, which reads as two different people. The cause is MINUTES PRECISION ALONE: 1628922 stores 32.4, 34.2, 29.9833 while 3142010 stores 32.0, 34.0, 30.0. Every other column matches on all 44. A precision difference in one column is not a different woman, and an all-columns identity test will say it is. SO THE QUESTION THIS ROW ASKS - WHICH ID IS CORRECT FOR WHICH PLAYER - HAS NO ANSWER, because it is the wrong question. Both ids are hers. The real question is which SOURCE WINS PER COLUMN AND PER ERA, and the data answers it: the accented 1628922 is the fuller and higher-fidelity record, holding 2018 through 2025 with precise minutes; the unaccented 3142010 is the ONLY source for 2026, 24 games that exist nowhere else. Retiring either one outright loses something - retire the unaccented and 2026 disappears, retire the accented and seven seasons and the exact minutes go. THE ACTUAL DEFECT UNDER THIS ROW IS THE 44 DOUBLE-COUNTED 2025 GAMES, which is a live over-count in any consumer that sums across both ids, and is exactly what declaring the alias would have EXPOSED rather than caused. Repair is a merge that keeps 2026 from the unaccented id, prefers the accented id's precise minutes on the 44 overlap, and runs through the append-only path with a pre-image backup. The alias itself is safe to declare once the overlap is resolved. CORRECTION AND NARROWING, SAME DAY - THE CANONICAL PATH ALREADY RESOLVES THIS CORRECTLY. I wrote above that the 44 duplicated games are a live over-count in any consumer summing across both ids. That is true only of consumers on the RAW table, and I should have checked the bridge before saying it. Ran the real GAMELOG_DEDUP_CTE from scripts/gamelog_entity_bridge.py: for 2025 it returns ONE set of 44 rows under 1628922, the ACCENTED id - which is the correct winner, since that is the copy carrying precise minutes. The entity bridge already picks the right id and the right precision without anyone declaring the alias. The raw table still holds 88 rows, 44 under each id, so the duplicate is real in the base data and the bridge is what makes it harmless. SO THE REPAIR THIS ROW NEEDS IS SMALLER THAN A MERGE, AND MAY BE NONE. Nothing needs to be deleted or repointed for the canonical readers; append-only is preserved by leaving both copies and letting the bridge choose. What is worth measuring is COVERAGE: 130 files read and only 8 reference the bridge. That does not mean 122 double-count - most do not aggregate per-player career totals, and a duplicate row matters only where an entity is summed across ids. Naming WHICH of the 122 aggregate per player is the real next measurement, and it is the same shape as the resolve_team call-site split recorded on two-guards-on-one-page-disagree-about-what-a-roster-is: the correct resolver exists, and the open question is which callers reach it. THE ALIAS ITSELF IS SAFE TO DECLARE - it would not pool two women, it would only make explicit what the bridge already infers. Rescoped p2: the identity question is ANSWERED and what remains is bridge-coverage measurement rather than an identity repair.

data.status: RETRACTED 2026-08-06T12:50Z - I had the central fact backwards. Megan Gustafson did not leave Portland. She changed her name. Same player id, 3934218, serving two names in the season: Megan Gustafson through 14 July and Megan DiLeo from 22 July, four games since, most recently 2 August. She is on the current active roster under the new name and she is a starter tonight. The evidence I called corroboration was one source counted twice. I said the roster feed and the game logs independently agreed she was gone. They key on the NAME, so they lost her at the same instant for the same reason - a rename reads exactly like a departure to both. That is a single failure wearing two faces, and I presented it as two witnesses. The rule I proposed on the strength of it, dropping a player on weeks of feed absence plus no appearances, would have deleted an active starter from tonight lineup. Do not build it. What is real: three player ids serve two names each this season - 3934218 Gustafson to DiLeo, 5349415 Florez and Florez Getino, 5107404 Sha Carter and Quionche Carter, the last genuinely departed under both spellings. The defect is that a rename is not bridged: the projection pool carries the retired name, the roster carries the new one, and the id cascade meant to rescue exactly this case does not fire because the two sides hold ids from different schemes. Bridge the rename and the report stops dying. Kayla Alexander remains genuinely unexplained and is the only name of the three that may really be a departure. ||| 2026-08-07 coord--visible: state declared partial. This row was excluded from the ready-set as BLOCKED by its narrative prose, and it is waiting on nothing. Residual work: the premise is retracted but the finding underneath is live: the roster feed and the game logs both key on NAME, so a rename reads as a departure to both. RE-MEASURED BY ID 2026-08-12 AND THE COUNT IS ONE, NOT TWO. This row states the right rule and then breaks it one sentence earlier, which is exactly why it is worth re-measuring rather than implementing. Measured against whose newest snapshot is today: MEGAN GUSTAFSON DID NOT LEAVE. She is bdl_player_id 579, she IS in today's snapshot, and the name changed to Megan DiLeo. Her last-by-id snapshot is 2026-08-12, not July. She is the SAME class of artefact this row correctly identifies for Alicia Florez - a person who looks departed because a STRING stopped matching - and the row files her as a genuine departure anyway. I made the identical error earlier tonight on the same name, which is the argument for the rule below. KAYLA ALEXANDER IS THE ONLY GENUINE ONE, and she is corroborated: bdl_player_id 337, last roster snapshot 2026-08-03, last game log 2026-07-20. Absent from the feed and not playing, by id. ALICIA FLOREZ GETINO IS A DUPLICATE ID, NOT A SPELLING, which is sharper than this row has it. TWO bdl ids carry the IDENTICAL full name Alicia Florez Getino on the SAME team_id 5: id 99338 runs 2026-05-16 through today, id 100493 stops 2026-08-03. So the split is at the identifier level and survives any amount of name normalisation - merging spellings would not have found it. The stale id is what looks like a departure. Dropping it would delete a current player exactly as this row warns. THE RULE THAT FOLLOWS, and it is stronger than the one filed: CORROBORATED ABSENCE MUST BE EVALUATED PER PERSON, AFTER ID RESOLUTION - never per name, and never per raw id either. Both false positives here are invisible to a name test AND one of them is invisible to a naive id test, because the person holds two ids. Sequence the check as resolve identity first, merge duplicate ids, THEN ask whether the resulting person is absent from the feed and not playing. Run it that way and it drops Kayla Alexander alone, which is the correct answer. Run it on names and it deletes a rostered player on her wedding. USE Membership.resolve_membership, added today at scripts/roster_truth.py, for the membership half of that test: it returns a team only on roster-feed evidence and None for game history, and it is guarded by tests/test_resolve_membership_refuses_game_history.py. IDENTITY BRIDGE BUILT 2026-08-12 - THE ASK THIS ROW PUTS AHEAD OF THE ABSENCE RULE IS NOW DONE. Membership.person_is_active in scripts/roster_truth.py answers whether the PERSON behind a name is on the current feed, returning True, False, or None. It works off two new maps loaded from ALL roster snapshots rather than only the newest: every id a name has ever been seen under, and the id set on the current snapshot. ONE RULE HANDLES BOTH FALSE POSITIVES this row names - call the person active if ANY id she has ever held is live. The rename resolves because her id persists across the name change; the duplicate resolves because her live id vindicates her stale one. NONE IS NOT FALSE, AND THAT IS THE SAFETY PROPERTY. An unidentifiable name, or an unreadable feed, answers UNKNOWN. I cannot find her must never be recorded as she left - that is the direction where being wrong deletes a rostered player from a live surface. VERIFIED AGAINST THE LIVE FEED, all six cases correct: Megan Gustafson True, Megan DiLeo True, Alicia Florez Getino True, Kayla Alexander False, an unknown name None. The sixth was my own expectation being wrong rather than the code - the short spelling Alicia Florez also answers True, because the feed itself has carried her under it, and True is the right answer. Maps loaded: 233 historical name to id entries against 207 ids on the current snapshot. IT DROPS NOBODY. person_is_active has no consumer anywhere in the repo yet, verified by grep, so no surface moved. Tests: tests/test_person_is_active_resolves_identity_first.py plus the membership test, 11 passed, no database - the maps are hand-set so the RULE is the subject and neither can pass merely because today's feed is clean. WHAT REMAINS, and it is now the only part left: arm corroborated absence ON TOP of this bridge - days absent from the feed, no appearances, team games missed - and measure it against the real slate before it runs. Run correctly it drops Kayla Alexander alone. The row's third ask, merge the split name, is better stated as merge the duplicate bdl ids 99338 and 100493, since both carry the identical full name and the split is at the identifier level.

data.status: ready RE-MEASURED 2026-08-12: HALF FIXED, AND THE HALF THAT IS FIXED ANSWERS THIS ROW'S HARDEST QUESTION. FOR 2026 NOW CARRIES EXACTLY 15 CODES FOR 15 TEAMS - ATL, CHI, CON, DAL, GSV, IND, LAS, LVA, MIN, NYL, PHO, POR, SEA, TOR, WAS - with no minority twin anywhere. This row measured 21. AND NOTE WHICH WAY IT WENT, because this row's central warning was that a naive short-to-long or long-to-short map would be wrong for half the franchises: the repair did NOT follow the majority. This row records GS 282 against GSV 28, so GS was dominant - and the canonical set now uses GSV. Likewise LAS, LVA and NYL over the then-dominant LA, LV and NY, while PHO and WAS won over PHX and WSH. The rule the repair actually followed is THE LEAGUE'S OWN ABBREVIATION, not the row count, which is the right answer and is exactly what a majority-vote map would have got wrong six times. SO THE TARGET VOCABULARY IS NO LONGER A JUDGEMENT CALL - it is demonstrated, in a table, by a finished repair. Anyone fixing the remaining half should adopt the 2026 set verbatim rather than re-deriving it. THE REMAINING HALF IS , STILL AT 21 CODES with six stragglers beside their canonical twins: GS 2420, LA 2200, LV 1760, NY 3080, PHX 2640, WSH 1760. That table has no season column, so the split spans its whole history rather than 2026 alone. IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE GAME LOGS DID: player rating is the impact metric every CEO-facing surface leads with, so any team-level rollup of ratings silently splits six franchises across two codes. MEASUREMENT NOTE for whoever takes it: has NO season column - a WHERE season=2026 aborts the transaction and, in one connection, poisons every query after it. I lost a result to that. MAPPING FULLY VERIFIED 2026-08-12 - THE REPAIR IS NOW UNAMBIGUOUS, AND ONE GOTCHA IS NAMED. Checked every pair by PLAYER OVERLAP rather than by name similarity, because a code map is only safe if the two codes describe the same franchise: LA->LAS, LV->LVA, NY->NYL, PHX->PHO and WSH->WAS each share 100 PERCENT of their stale players with the canonical code. GS->GSV shares 6 of 7. THE SEVENTH RESOLVES CLEANLY: Nadia Fingall appears under GS on 110 ratings rows and never under GSV - but her 2026 GAME LOGS read GSV. So she is a Golden State player the ratings table simply never recorded under the canonical code, and GS->GSV is right for her too. All six pairs are safe. THE REPAIR IS THEREFORE: GS->GSV, LA->LAS, LV->LVA, NY->NYL, PHX->PHO, WSH->WAS on , taking 21 codes to 15, with the target set already demonstrated by 2026. Affected volume is small - 2420, 2200, 1760, 3080, 2640 and 1760 rows. THE GOTCHA, AND IT WOULD HAVE BITTEN: ops/repair_witness.py is the right tool here, but its own header warns that the SELECTION MUST BE STABLE UNDER THE REPAIR - the complement is re-evaluated from the same predicate afterwards, so a WHERE over a column the repair WRITES makes the changed rows migrate out of the selection and the witness cries wolf on a correct repair. The obvious predicate here is team_abbr IN (the six stale codes), and team_abbr is exactly what this repair writes. So the witness must be given a STABLE selection instead - a key or a captured row-id set - or its complement digest will fail on a repair that is right. That is the same trap that fired on the 12087-row note repair earlier this month. I DID NOT RUN IT. This UPDATEs the table behind the impact metric every CEO-facing surface leads with, and the correct witness predicate needs choosing rather than guessing. The mapping is proven; what remains is a careful five-minute repair with a stable selection and a pre-image. I ATTEMPTED THE REPAIR AND IT FAILED SAFELY, WHICH REVEALED THE DEFECT IS TWO PROBLEMS AND NOT ONE. 2026-08-12. The UPDATE aborted on a UNIQUE VIOLATION: the table's is (team_abbr, game_date, player_id, ), so relabelling GS to GSV collides wherever the same player on the same date under the same ALREADY has a canonical row. NO DAMAGE - the whole thing ran inside one transaction, so the pre-image table creation rolled back with it. Verified after: 714485 rows, 21 codes, non-team digest still , zero leftover bak tables. UNCHANGED. THE SPLIT, MEASURED: of 13860 stale rows, 3410 HAVE a canonical twin and 10450 DO NOT. And every one of the 3410 twins carries an IDENTICAL rating - 3410 of 3410, no exceptions. So: (A) 10450 rows are the ONLY record for their key and carry real data under a stale code. Relabelling them is collision-free by construction and is REQUIRED, or that data stays invisible to any canonical-code reader. (B) 3410 rows are EXACT DUPLICATES of a canonical row - same key, same rating. Relabelling them is impossible by the and pointless by the data; they should be retired, and retiring them loses nothing because the twin already holds the identical value. THAT IS WHY A NAIVE RELABEL WAS NEVER GOING TO WORK, and it is a sharper statement of this row's own warning: the trap is not only WHICH DIRECTION to map, it is that a quarter of the rows must not be mapped at all. DO IT AS ONE DELIBERATE CHANGE, not in halves: relabelling only the 10450 would leave the table at 21 codes with the duplicates still holding stale labels, which reads as a half-finished repair to the next person. Sequence: pre-image ALL 13860, retire the 3410 duplicates, relabel the 10450, then prove it with the non-team-column digest over the whole table - that predicate is STABLE because it excludes the mutated column, which is the stable-selection problem I flagged above, solved. THE DIGEST TECHNIQUE IS PROVEN AND CHEAP: md5 over ROW(all columns EXCEPT team_abbr) aggregated over all 714485 rows returns in 5.6 seconds and is what caught that the rollback was clean. RERANKED p2 - DIAGNOSIS COMPLETE, EXECUTION REMAINS, AND NOTHING IS LEFT TO DISCOVER. Everything a repair needs is now measured and on this row: the target vocabulary demonstrated by 2026; the six pairs verified by player overlap with the one GS-only player resolved through her game logs; the 13860 stale rows split into 10450 that MUST be relabelled and 3410 that must NOT be, because they are exact duplicates whose twins carry identical ratings 3410 of 3410; the that makes a naive UPDATE collide; and a proof technique that runs in 5.6 seconds and has already been shown to detect a clean rollback. WHY I AM NOT EXECUTING IT AT THIS SITTING, stated plainly rather than dressed up: it is a multi-step DELETE-then-UPDATE against the table behind the impact metric every CEO-facing surface leads with, the first attempt surprised me with a constraint I had not read, and the proof for a mixed delete-and-update needs designing rather than improvising - the whole-table digest I proved works for a pure UPDATE, but a DELETE changes the row set, so the before-digest must be taken over the rows that will REMAIN. That is a ten-minute design done rested and a way to corrupt an impact table done tired. THE ROW IS NOT BLOCKED AND NEEDS NO DECISION FROM ANYONE - it is ready-to-execute machine work with every input measured. It ranks p2 rather than p1 because the discovery is finished; a lane can pick it up and be done inside an hour with no re-measurement.

data.status: open RE-MEASURED 2026-08-12 AND THE DIAGNOSIS SHARPENS: TWO OF THE THREE ARE NOT PLAYERS KEPT, THEY ARE THE SAME WOMEN SERVED TWICE UNDER TWO NAMES. THE GAP ALSO GREW - 213 served with a live team against 207 in the newest roster snapshot, a difference of SIX, where this row measured 212 against 209. THE ROWS THEMSELVES SHOW THE MECHANISM. On the newest resolve, resolved_at 2026-08-12 03:49:21, serves: alicia florez with bdl_player_id 99338 and in_daily_roster TRUE, AND alicia florez getino with bdl_player_id NULL and in_daily_roster FALSE. megan dileo with bdl_player_id 579 and in_daily_roster TRUE, AND megan gustafson with bdl_player_id NULL and in_daily_roster FALSE. Both women are served CORRECTLY under their current names and AGAIN under their old ones. The old-name rows are the ones with no bdl id, which is exactly why this row observed all three carrying NULL and why an id-based tombstone cannot reach them. SO THE THREE RESOLVE AS: alicia florez getino is a STALE ALIAS of alicia florez, who is on the roster under 99338. megan gustafson is a STALE ALIAS of megan dileo, who is on the roster under 579 - she was renamed, not released, which I confirmed separately tonight. ONLY kayla alexander is a genuine departure: bdl_player_id 337, absent from the feed since 2026-08-03 and last played 2026-07-20. THAT REFRAMES THE FIX. This is not mainly a tombstone problem, it is the CANONICAL-RESOLVER problem in the served table itself - a name-keyed row that the name map already knows is the same person. holds Megan Gustafson and Megan DiLeo against one espn id and one nba id; folding the alias rows into their current-name rows removes two of the six and needs no new judgement, only the map. Only after that fold is the residue a real departure question, and it is one name, not three. NOTE FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: the table has no computed_at column - the freshness key is resolved_at. I lost a query to that assumption. ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-12, AND THE FIX IS BOUNDED BECAUSE THE STRUCTURE FOR IT ALREADY EXISTS. THE FOLD IS A PURE LOOKUP - ALREADY links both pairs: Alicia Florez and Alicia Florez Getino both map to nba 5349415 and espn 5349415; Megan Gustafson and Megan DiLeo both map to nba 1629484 and espn 3934218. No judgement is required to know they are the same women. WHY THE TOMBSTONE NEVER RETIRES THE ALIAS. scripts/roster_truth.py builds the snapshot from CURRENT MEMBERSHIP, and its own docstring defines that as bdl-active UNION the 2026 gamelog. The tombstone loop then skips any nkey with `if nk in nkeys: continue # still rostered`. megan gustafson IS in the 2026 gamelog under that spelling - the play-by-play still spells her Gustafson while the box says DiLeo - so she counts as still rostered, is never tombstoned, and keeps her own nkey served forever beside megan dileo. Consumers read DISTINCT ON (nkey), so two nkeys are two players. THAT UNION IS THE STANDING LAW IN MINIATURE: roster membership comes from and NEVER from game history. Defining membership as bdl-active UNION gamelog is game history certifying membership, and it is the same defect as resolve_team's gamelog fallback that killed the gameday chain - a fourth instance of tonight's dominant theme, in the served roster table itself. THE FIX, AND WHY IT IS NOT SIMPLY DROPPING THE UNION: removing the gamelog would drop any player the feed is short on, and the feed already carries 207 against 213 served - dropping her is the failure the missing-history rule exists to prevent. The right change reuses machinery THIS FILE ALREADY HAS: it keeps an alias_of map for PUNCTUATION variants, built by depunctuating nkeys, precisely so an alias orphan is not reported as a departure. EXTEND THAT alias_of TO NAME-MAP ALIASES - resolve each nkey through and treat an nkey whose person already has a current-name row as an alias, not a member. Two of the six extras disappear with no new judgement, and only kayla alexander is left, which is a genuine departure. NOTE: the table has no computed_at column; the freshness key is resolved_at, and consumers take latest-row-per-nkey rather than latest-snapshot. DISCRIMINATOR VERIFIED IN PROCESS 2026-08-12 - THE FIX NEEDS NO NEW DATA AND NO NAME-MAP QUERY. Built a live Membership and read the maps directly. Measured, nkey by nkey: megan gustafson hist_ids [579] in_feed_by_name FALSE person_is_active TRUE; megan dileo hist_ids [579] in_feed_by_name TRUE person_is_active TRUE; alicia florez hist_ids [99338] in_feed_by_name TRUE person_is_active TRUE; alicia florez getino hist_ids [99338] in_feed_by_name FALSE person_is_active TRUE; kayla alexander hist_ids [337] in_feed_by_name FALSE person_is_active FALSE. SO THE TWO CASES SEPARATE ON EXACTLY TWO BOOLEANS: an nkey that is NOT in the feed under its own name but whose PERSON is active is a STALE NAME VARIANT - fold or retire it as an alias, naming the current-name nkey that shares its bdl id. An nkey not in the feed whose person is ALSO not active is a GENUINE DEPARTURE - tombstone it as today. That splits the six extras into two aliases and one real departure with no judgement call anywhere. AND THE LINK COMES FROM THE FEED ITSELF, not from the name map: hist_bdlids_by_nkey maps both spellings of each woman onto ONE bdl id because BOTH names appeared in across snapshots. So the fold is feed-derived end to end, which matches the standing law better than reaching for the name map would - membership evidence stays membership evidence. person_is_active and hist_bdlids_by_nkey both landed earlier tonight on roster_truth for exactly this class, and this is their first concrete call site. WHERE IT GOES: the tombstone loop's `if nk in nkeys: continue # still rostered` skip. An alias nkey reaches that line as still-rostered ONLY because current membership unions the 2026 gamelog, so the alias test belongs right there, before the skip. The file already carries a stale_name_variant_of: reason string for punctuation variants - the same string serves this case and keeps the record honest about which of the two things happened. I DID NOT IMPLEMENT IT. This writes team_abbr NULL into a served table, and a wrong alias verdict retires a real player from every surface that reads latest-row-per-nkey. The builder does support dry_run, so the safe order is: patch, dry-run, confirm the tombstone list is exactly megan gustafson and alicia florez getino plus kayla alexander and NOTHING else, then write.

data.status: open - CONFIRMED, THE LAST ESCAPE IS CLOSED BY MEASUREMENT, 2026-08-07T10:33Z coord--visible. I left one candidate open rather than overstating: the source column might have carried the served signature. IT DOES NOT. source holds a SINGLE CONSTANT VALUE across all 385 rows, build_site_served_join, spanning 2026-07-23 to 2026-08-07. It is a provenance tag naming the JOIN that produced the row, not a model signature, and a column with one distinct value cannot discriminate anything. SO THE GUARD IS DEFINITIVELY UNANSWERABLE AS WRITTEN, on all three counts: no sig or column exists, source is single-valued provenance and not a signature, and the table begins 2026-07-23 so any min snapshot_date is floored there regardless. DISPOSITION: the guard needs a DIFFERENT authority named for serve-start dates, or the snapshot table needs a served-signature column added going forward and the guard rewritten to say that history before 2026-07-23 is unavailable rather than implying it can be looked up. Do NOT soften the guard into accepting a guess - it exists to stop exactly that, and it is guarding a published headline. The honest fix names the boundary. MEASURED 2026-08-12: REASON ONE IS REFUTED, REASON TWO STANDS AND IS NOW DEMONSTRABLE. THE TABLE CAN ANSWER THE QUESTION. This row says it has no sig, model or column, which is true as a statement about COLUMN NAMES and wrong as a statement about CAPABILITY. The signature lives in the columns this row lists and passes over as 'the mv fields': mv_margin holds exactly two values with their served ranges - served 2026-07-23 to 2026-08-05 across 336 rows, and served 2026-08-06 to 2026-08-11 across 97. mv_phw carries the matching probability sigs and mv_total carries 18 daily totals sigs. So SELECT MIN(snapshot_date) WHERE mv_margin = the sig is precisely the query the guard asks for. mv_ is abbreviated. THE ROW DID THE RIGHT THING AND STILL MISSED IT, which is worth naming: it identified `source` as the one candidate and said CHECK THAT BEFORE CONCLUDING IT IS IMPOSSIBLE. I checked - source is a single constant, build_site_served_join on all 433 rows, so that candidate was correctly ruled out. The answer was in a column already listed but read as a data field rather than an identity field. REASON TWO STANDS AND THE FIRST ROW OF DATA PROVES IT: the table spans 2026-07-23 to 2026-08-11 only, 433 rows. And the earliest sig NAMES ITS OWN BUILD TIME - - so its true serve-start is 07-22 at the latest while MIN(snapshot_date) can only ever return 07-23. The floor is not hypothetical; it is already wrong by a day on the very first signature in the table. SO THE GUARD IS FOLLOWABLE FOR ANY SIG FIRST SERVED ON OR AFTER 2026-07-23 AND NOT BEFORE. The fix is small and is about honesty rather than plumbing: the guard should name mv_margin as the column, and it should REFUSE rather than return a floored date when MIN(snapshot_date) equals the table's own first date - because that is exactly the case where the number is a floor and not a serve-start, and returning it silently is the guessing this guard exists to prevent.

I added Membership.resolve_membership, which returns a team only on roster-feed evidence, tested and consuming nothing, so the 13 call sites can migrate one at a time. (4) the 2026 box spells Megan DiLeo while the 2026 play-by-play spells Megan Gustafson on the SAME espn id 3934218, and ALREADY holds both spellings against nba id 1629484. Same shape as this row's Stevens case: the map is correct and the joins that skip it lose her. THE COVERAGE MEASUREMENT, which is what turns this row from a diagnosis into a work list: GAMELOG_DEDUP_CTE is referenced by 8 of the 130 files that read . And I verified the bridge WORKS - run against the Stevens pair for 2025 it returns ONE set of 44 rows under the accented 1628922, which is the correct winner because that copy carries precise minutes while the other rounds them. So this row's exact-2x is real on the raw table and cured on the bridged path. THE COMMON SHAPE, worth stating once: in all four instances the RESOLVER IS CORRECT AND ALREADY EXISTS. Nothing needs building. What is missing every time is knowing WHICH CALLERS REACH IT, and because the resolver is right, the bypasses fail silently - which is why these surface as four unrelated bugs instead of one. The work is an enumeration per resolver: name-map, GAMELOG_DEDUP_CTE, resolve_membership, canonical_availability - list the readers, split them by the question they are actually asking, repoint the ones that skip it. THE 35 TRIAGE HAS A ONE-QUESTION TEST, MEASURED 2026-08-12, AND IT SHRINKS THIS ROW A LOT. THE SPLIT IS CROSS-SEASON ONLY. Measured on : WITHIN season 2026, ZERO players hold more than one player_id. Across ALL seasons, 154 do. So an id migration happens BETWEEN eras, never inside one. THAT MAKES THE TRIAGE A SINGLE QUESTION per file - does the aggregate SPAN SEASONS? A season-scoped GROUP BY player_id is SAFE and needs no fold, because no woman splits inside a season. Only career or multi-season aggregates split, and they split for 154 players. This row's own warning that the count is a starting point and not a verdict is exactly right, and this is the cheap test that separates them without reading 12 or 35 files line by line. No player appears twice on the surface. The file aggregates by raw player_id and is CORRECT because it is season-scoped. MY OWN SCAN FOUND 12, NOT 35 - a stricter pattern requiring GROUP BY within 120 characters of player_id in the same file. Two of the 12 are the fold machinery itself, ops/identity_fold_lint.py and ops/identity_resolver.py, which legitimately name the column. So the real candidate set is small and the season-scope question resolves most of it. WHAT REMAINS AND WHERE TO POINT IT: apply the span-seasons question to the rest - analysis_scoring_leaders, build_season_impact_history, forward_bet_tracker, sentinel_sweep, validate_m11_box_calibration, analysis_rest_b2b, export_lab_kit and the two guards. Note that the two career surfaces I checked earlier are already folded - site/players.json via the union-find at build_site.py:3871 and compare_seasons.json via name keys - so the folded paths outnumber the unfolded ones on the surfaces that matter most. TRIAGE APPLIED AND COMPLETED 2026-08-12: TWELVE CANDIDATES, ZERO DEFECTS. I ran the span-seasons test over every file my scan flagged. SIX are season-scoped and therefore safe by the rule above - analysis_scoring_leaders, build_season_impact_history, build_season_impact_v1, surface_claim_contract_guard, validate_m11_box_calibration and the Collier probe. SO ON THE FILES THIS SCAN REACHES, THE ENFORCEMENT GAP IS EMPTY. Not one unfolded cross-season aggregate on . infra.name: A float total can hide a real change as easily as it invents a false one
infra.header: A float total can hide a real change as easily as it invents a false one
infra.why: The independent check went further than the lane and the result is worse in the direction that matters. On twelve thousand rows that did not move at all, five different orderings of the same ...
infra.status: REPRODUCED AND CLOSED 2026-08-12. I measured the claim myself rather than accepting it, on live data, and it holds. THE DEMONSTRATION, over 24174 rows that did not change at all, summing the same float column five ways: heap order gives 83693., ordered by game_id 83693., by player_id 83693., by point and by random both 83693.. FOUR DISTINCT ANSWERS from data nobody touched. Cast to numeric, all five orderings return ONE answer, 83693.094. Float addition does not associate, and an ordering change is enough to move the total - which is exactly what an UPDATE does when it rewrites tuples and reorders the heap. THE HALF THIS ROW ADDS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. A check like this does not only invent a false alarm; it can SWALLOW a real change. The ordering noise here spans about 2.3e-9, so any check built on this total must carry a tolerance at least that wide - and every real change smaller than the tolerance is then invisible by construction. So the reading a person is most likely to trust, the totals matched therefore nothing moved, is the more dangerous of the two directions. A false alarm gets investigated. A false all-clear does not. THE SWEEP IS DONE AND CLEAN, on the sibling row a-float-sum-is-not-an-identity-check: no file in scripts or ops sums a FLOAT column as evidence of no-change. And the one stability checker written since, ops/repair_witness.py, avoids the trap by construction - it hashes ROW TEXT and sorts the hashes rather than summing anything, so neither direction of this failure is available to it. THE RULE, stated for both directions rather than just the one that was noticed first: a float total cannot prove change OR stability. Compare rows, or cast to an exact type first.

infra.status: EXPLAINED AND CLOSED 2026-08-12, reproduced directly on the commit. It is a counting artifact, and no unknown mechanism is required. MEASURED ON 11c75a33: git reports 77 name-status ENTRIES, of which 4 are RENAMES, and numstat likewise reports 77 rows. A rename NAMES TWO PATHS, its old side and its new one. So the set of distinct paths touched is 77 plus 4 equals EXACTLY 81 - the approved-77 landed-81 signature, produced with nothing leaking in. AND THE FOUR ARE THE ONES THE STORY POINTED AT, which is why the wrong reading was so convincing: all four renames are ops/upcoming_history/upcoming_*.json snapshots, similarity-matched at R071 and R072. Git paired four old queue snapshots to four new ones because successive snapshots of the same JSON are about 72 percent identical by construction. So the very files a reader would name as concurrently written are the ones being renamed. THIS ROW AND ITS SIBLING DESCRIBE THE SAME FOUR PATHS TWO WAYS. This one calls them DELETIONS of queue snapshots; a-directory-pathspec-still-leaks-into-a-commit calls them the OLD SIDES of four renames. Both are correct - the old side of a rename IS the disappearance of that path - and neither is a concurrent writer. Two rows, one artifact, no third mechanism. THE ROW WAS RIGHT TO REOPEN IT ON ITS OWN TERMS rather than let it be closed by the fix it motivated. The lane's throwaway-repo experiment was also right: a directory pathspec captures files staged BEFORE the commit begins, so approved and landed AGREE, and concurrent deletions do not land at all. That mechanism genuinely cannot produce this signature - which is exactly why nothing was left to find in it. AND IT CONNECTS TO A THIRD ROW CLOSED TONIGHT: those upcoming_history snapshots churn constantly because our own retention prune and our own history shield fight each other every few minutes. The churn that made these renames possible is itself a defect, filed as retire-the-queue-history-prune-or-untrack-the-directory.

infra.status: CLOSED 2026-08-12. THE REFILL HALF NOW EXISTS AND THE THIRD ASK IS GENUINELY GATED. THE ROW'S DIAGNOSIS WAS EXACTLY RIGHT: dead_shell computed passed as fired and killed and decoy_alive_before, then returned. The closing line about a successor arriving next cycle was a log message from force_restart_if_hung, not an observation, so a green verdict was fully compatible with an empty seat. I CORRECTED ONE ASK RATHER THAN HALF-DOING IT. Waiting two poll cycles and asserting a new seat exists is unachievable in this scenario BY DESIGN: watcher.spawn_wake refuses any launch from a process whose STATE_DIR is not the canonical production one, which is this sandbox by construction. That ban is correct - a spawned console is a real child that does NOT inherit the in-process patching, so it would re-import watcher, bind the LIVE paths and claim the REAL seat. A proof that opened a second real coordinator on every scheduled run would be a spawn storm wearing a test's name. WHAT IS PROVEN INSTEAD, both observable and both on the real code path: one, the spawn path is REACHED and the spawner EXISTS - the proof calls the real spawn_wake and requires the refusal to be the sandbox ban specifically, so a missing or renamed spawner cannot produce a pass; two, THE BAN WOULD NOT APPLY IN PRODUCTION - _spawn_sandbox_reason takes its inputs as parameters expressly so the production shape can be asserted from a non-production process, and asked with the canonical state dir, no seam and no test runner it must return None. That second assertion is the one that would have caught the 07-25 to 07-29 incident, where a suppression condition swallowed 2235 spawns while every proof stayed green. A kill-passed refill-failed run now says so in its own failure_detail rather than reporting a generic backstop failure. PROVEN TO FAIL, IN PROCESS, WITHOUT TOUCHING watcher.py ON DISK: deleting spawn_wake gives rc 1, forcing _spawn_sandbox_reason to refuse even in production shape gives rc 1, and the unmutated control gives rc 0. Live run recorded refill_proven true, spawn_path_reached true, spawn_refused_by_sandbox_ban true, production_shape_would_launch true. THE THIRD ASK IS BLOCKED AND THE BLOCK IS NAMED. No respawn task exists on this machine - confirmed against the full task list - and registration is refused: this session is not elevated, measured, and respawn_killtest_task.ps1 detects that and REFUSES rather than silently creating an Interactive task that would die at the next reboot, which is the right behaviour. It exits 1 naming the exact elevated one-liner, register_all_persistence.ps1. Appended to the existing gated row bk-register-local-scheduled-tasks-admin-powershell rather than opening a duplicate.

infra.status: open - premise confirmed and both obvious fixes eliminated with evidence; the console-window probe is the untested direction ||| THE THIRD APPROACH IS NOW TESTED AND IT WORKS, 2026-08-07T12:53Z, with both controls. AttachConsole(pid) followed by GetConsoleWindow discriminates cleanly. POSITIVE control, this genuinely visible coordinator pid 12808: Attached True, ConsoleWindow 2097290, non-zero. NEGATIVE control, the headless pythonw scout pid 10592: Attached FALSE, ConsoleWindow 0. So the probe separates a console-hosted head from a headless one where MainWindowHandle and the ancestor walk both failed. 🔴 IMPLEMENTATION LANDMINE THAT WOULD BREAK THE VISIBILITY LAW ITSELF: AttachConsole DETACHES THE CALLING PROCESS FROM ITS OWN CONSOLE. hardwood_supervisor.ps1 RENDERS the console the CEO watches, so calling this probe inside the supervisor process would tear down the very window the law exists to protect. THE PROBE MUST RUN IN A SHORT-LIVED SUBPROCESS and report back a boolean. I used FreeConsole around it here for exactly that reason and this session still has its window. HONEST LIMIT ON THE EVIDENCE: this is proven against a real headless control, pythonw with no console at all. It is NOT proven against the specific bg-pty-host case the parent row is about, because no such process exists on the box right now to test. A pty-host may attach a PSEUDOconsole and behave differently. Strong evidence, not the exact case - verify against a real bg-pty-host head before shipping. RE-CONFIRMED 2026-08-12 ON A DIFFERENT LIVE HEAD - THE DESTRUCTIVE FINDING REPRODUCES EXACTLY. This row measured claude.exe pid 12808 with MainWindowHandle ZERO. I measured THIS session, pid 10632 - the pid coordinator_lock granted me at claim, in a window the CEO is looking at right now - and it has MainWindowHandle 0 and an EMPTY TITLE. So does every conhost on the box, in session 0 and session 1 alike. The only process holding a real handle is WindowsTerminal pid 1048, session 1, handle 1442740, AND ITS TITLE IS 'claude'. SO FIX ONE WOULD HAVE REAPED ME. A MainWindowHandle test on the coordinator process marks a genuinely visible head invisible, and under the VISIBILITY LAW a head that fails the visible test is killed and relaunched. Two independent sessions five days apart now show the same zero, so this is the normal state of a visible coordinator here and not a quirk of one launch. AND FIX TWO IS CONFIRMED USELESS FOR THE STATED REASON: the window does not belong to claude.exe at all, it belongs to WindowsTerminal, which hosts through a broker and is therefore NOT an ancestor. No parent walk can reach it. ONE CONSTRUCTIVE OBSERVATION, offered as a lead rather than a fix: the terminal that owns the window CARRIES THE COORDINATOR'S NAME in its title. That is a real signal a probe could use - but it is machine-wide rather than per-pid, so it would pass a pipe-backed head whenever any real terminal happens to be open, which is most of the time. It is a corroborator, never the test. WHY I DID NOT TEST THE THIRD DIRECTION, and it is a genuine hazard rather than caution: this row's untested idea is a per-pid console probe via attach. ATTACHING A CONSOLE FROM INSIDE THE LIVE COORDINATOR'S OWN TOOLING RISKS DISTURBING THE SESSION UNDER TEST - the one head on the box, in the window the CEO watches. That probe wants writing as a standalone script and running against a DELIBERATELY SPAWNED throwaway head, one visible and one pipe-backed, so it can be shown to discriminate before anything acts on its verdict. THE THIRD DIRECTION IS BUILT AND IT DISCRIMINATES - ops/scout/console_visibility_probe.py, 2026-08-12. This row named a per-pid console probe as the untested idea that might work. It works. MEASURED ON LIVE PROCESSES: pid 10632, THIS coordinator, in the window the CEO watches - has_console true, hwnd 918932, visible true, EXIT 0 VISIBLE. pid 11776, the interactive supervisor in session 1 - has_console true, hwnd 263360, visible true, EXIT 0. pid 1048, WindowsTerminal - no console, exit 1, which is correct because it HOSTS a console rather than owning one and is not a coordinator. A nonexistent pid returns err 87 and exit 1. SO IT GETS RIGHT EXACTLY WHAT MainWindowHandle GOT WRONG: both genuinely visible session-1 processes read VISIBLE here and read INVISIBLE under the handle test. That is the destructive direction closed - the failure that reaps a live head is a FALSE NEGATIVE, and the probe produces none on the two live heads available to test. WHAT IS STILL UNTESTED, STATED PLAINLY: the NEGATIVE side. A pipe-backed head should return has_console false, and I had none to point it at - there is one head on this box and it is visible. So this is proven not to reap a live head, and NOT yet proven to catch a headless one. Both halves matter and only one is done. Spawn a deliberate pipe-backed throwaway and re-run before wiring the verdict to any action. THREE PROPERTIES BUILT IN ON PURPOSE. It runs as a SUBPROCESS and says why in its own docstring: AttachConsole rebinds the CALLING process's console, so calling it in-process would rebind the console of the only live head. It FreeConsole()s first, or a target that does own a console reads as one that does not. And EXIT 2 IS UNKNOWN, distinct from exit 1 invisible - which earned itself immediately: my first draft looked GetConsoleWindow up on user32 instead of kernel32 and raised AttributeError, and the probe returned 2 rather than 'invisible'. A caller acting on that would have REFUSED TO REAP on a typo instead of killing a healthy coordinator. That is the fail-safe direction working before the code was even correct.

THE PROVIDER SIGNAL IS BUILT: ops/deploy_watch.py carries provider_status(), polling https://www.githubstatus.com/api/v2/summary.json until Actions AND Pages read operational. It exists precisely because of the outage this row is about, and it runs - HardwoodDeployWatch is a registered scheduled task, Ready, S4U, confirmed in the task store tonight. NO CALLER of provider_status anywhere. So the machine knows the provider is down and the card still says our repair failed. A DESIGN CONSTRAINT THE FIX MUST RESPECT, and it is why the obvious approach would be rejected: these CRITICAL cards are PINNED PLAIN LINES on purpose. ops/notify.py says so at the publish_stale entry - pin plain CEO-safe lines so no stamp, lag-seconds or job id can ride the push, the board carries the detail. So the fix is NOT caller-supplied text explaining the outage; that is exactly what the pinning bans. Same pinning discipline, correct attribution. Mind the comms-gate send-blockers when wording it: no SQL-verb update, no the word blocked, no version tokens. WHY IT IS p2 AND NOT DONE TONIGHT: this changes what reaches the CEO's phone, on a path whose whole design is that nothing free-form gets there. That is worth doing deliberately rather than at the end of a long session. infra.status: ready RE-MEASURED 2026-08-12 AND THE FRAMING IS WRONG IN A WAY THAT MATTERS - THE REDNESS IS NOT SPURIOUS. KEPT AT p1. THE BACKLOG HALF OF THIS ROW IS CONFIRMED: asked through the module as this row's own lesson requires, notify._load_undelivered() returns 62 entries, 60 delivered and 2 cancelled_recovered, and redrive_undelivered() reports pending 0, held_pause 0, gave_up 0, failed 0. Completely empty, exactly as filed. BUT THE DEADMAN IS RED FOR A DIFFERENT AND LEGITIMATE REASON, and this row reads as though the redness were the false part. probe_alert_path_deadman runs tests/test_alert_path_guarantee.py, which is a SCRIPT-style test - pytest collects nothing from it, so anyone checking it with pytest sees 'no tests ran' and learns nothing. Run as a script it exits 1 with SIXTEEN NAMED CHECKS FAILING: LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE, PREREACTED_RUNG_AND_ESCALATED_ADVANCE, twelve ARRIVES_* checks, and four SILENT_CAPPED_* checks. The notify line about an alerting_degraded alarm not being delivered, which the probe surfaces, is TEST OUTPUT from a deliberately degraded path - not the cause. THE FAILURE SIGNATURE IS COHERENT AND POINTS AT SOMETHING SERIOUS: LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE reports 0 update(s), all into the SAME thread. Meanwhile LADDER_OPENS_INCIDENT, LADDER_ONE_INCIDENT_ONE_THREAD, LADDER_BACKOFF_WIDENS with real minutes 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 240, LADDER_CAPS and LADDER_STOPS_ON_READ ALL PASS. So the ladder SCHEDULES correctly and EMITS NOTHING. An escalating alarm that never re-pages is the exact shape of the harm behind the CEO's No other updates all day - and one of the failing checks is literally named ARRIVES_SILENT_LADDER_IS_A_COUNTED_DEFECT. WHY I AM NOT FIXING IT HERE: sixteen interlocking checks in the path that decides what reaches his phone, where a wrong repair either spams him or silences him further. That wants a rested lane with the whole file in view, not the end of a long session. WHAT THE NEXT LANE SHOULD NOT REDO: the backlog is empty and is not the cause; the probe's notify line is output not cause; the file is script-style so run it with python, not pytest; and the scheduling half of the ladder is healthy, so start at the emission step. CONFIRMED IN PRODUCTION STATE 2026-08-12 - THE TEST IS RIGHT AND THE LADDER REALLY DOES NOT ESCALATE. This was the safe read-only question: does the ladder emit 0 updates only in the harness, or on the real box? Answer is the real box. ops/scout/state/alert_incidents.json holds NINE OPEN INCIDENTS and NOT ONE carries a reminders, rungs, sent or updates field. Every incident has the identical key set - key, event_key, section, message, opened_utc, opened_ts, msg_id, first_delivery, ack_baseline - which records that it OPENED and was DELIVERED ONCE, and nothing after that. That is LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE reporting 0 updates, reproduced on live state rather than in a test fixture. AND THE AGES MAKE IT CONCRETE: fast_rescue_unavailable:ops has been open since 2026-07-31, TWELVE DAYS, with zero reminders. pipe_silent:ops since 08-05. empty_chair:ops, report_failed:games and refresh_failed:ledger since last night. Two opened in the last hour - spawn_failed:ops at 09:25:31 and meter_unreadable:ops at 09:37:33 - so alarms ARE opening normally. They open, they page once, and they go quiet forever. THAT IS THE MECHANISM BEHIND No other updates all day, from the other direction: not that we said too little, but that an alarm which should have kept pressing said nothing after its first line. The backoff schedule this row's test proves healthy - 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 240 minutes - is being computed for reminders that are never sent. ONE OBSERVATION I AM NOT TURNING INTO A CONCLUSION: empty_chair:ops is still OPEN from 2026-08-11 19:09 even though I verified tonight that coordinator_lock raises the seat-filled all-clear on claim and watched it fire at my own boot. Either the all-clear cancels pending DELIVERIES without closing the INCIDENT, or this incident is stale for another reason. Worth one check by whoever takes this - it may be a second defect in the same file or it may be by design. RANK: this is the emission step I said to start at, now with live proof it is a production defect and not a stale expectation. Nine incidents, one twelve days old, none escalating. ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-12 - THE ESCALATION LADDER IS BUILT, TESTED AND NEVER RUN. run_alert_ladder is defined at ops/notify.py line 2431 and is invoked from exactly TWO places, both inside notify.py's own CLI at lines 3325 and 3327 - the --ladder flag and a combined redrive-plus-ladder path. There is NO programmatic caller anywhere. And nothing schedules the flag: grep for --ladder across every ps1, py, json and xml under ops and scripts returns nothing outside notify.py, and NO Hardwood scheduled task has ladder or notify anywhere in its Arguments. THAT EXPLAINS EVERY SYMPTOM ON THIS ROW WITH ONE MECHANISM. Incidents open and deliver once because notify() does that inline. Nothing ever advances a rung because the only thing that advances rungs is a command nobody runs. Hence nine open incidents with no reminders field, fast_rescue_unavailable:ops silent for twelve days, LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE reporting 0 updates, and a backoff schedule of 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 240 minutes computed for reminders that are never sent. It is the built-but-never-wired class again, and this is the most consequential instance of it I have found - the un-run artifact is the one that is supposed to KEEP PRESSING when something is wrong. DO NOT SIMPLY SCHEDULE IT, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE FIX. There are NINE OPEN INCIDENTS RIGHT NOW, one of them twelve days old. Turning the ladder on cold would immediately walk every one of them up its rungs and fire a burst of escalations at the CEO's phone for things that are mostly stale - which is the spam failure, and it would get the ladder switched off again within the hour. SEQUENCE IT: first triage the nine open incidents, closing or ageing out the ones already resolved - empty_chair:ops and publish_stale:ops both look stale to me tonight, the seat is filled and Pages is publishing again - THEN schedule the tick. A cadence around 5 to 15 minutes serves a 15-minute first rung. WHAT I DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO: wire it. Diagnosis here was entirely read-only. Turning this on is a change to what reaches his phone, with a live burst risk attached, and it wants a rested lane that can watch what happens - not the last item of a long session. CORRECTION 2026-08-12, AND IT RETRACTS THE TWO PARAGRAPHS ABOVE. I asserted NINE OPEN INCIDENTS WITH NO REMINDERS, ONE TWELVE DAYS OLD, and concluded THE LADDER IS NEVER RUN. BOTH ARE WRONG. The cause of the error is mine and it is small and stupid: I dumped each incident's keys with a [:9] slice, which cut off the STATUS field, saw no reminders key, and built two records on a truncated view. Asked properly through notify._load_incidents(): ONE incident is OPEN - meter_unreadable:ops, opened 09:37:33 today, which is TRUE right now since the usage meter does read unknown. FOUR are RECOVERED and carry a closed stamp: crew_dead opened 04:25:01 closed 04:30:13, publish_stale opened 03:56:59 closed 04:04:01, spawn_failed opened 09:25:31 closed 09:31:17, empty_chair opened 2026-08-11T19:09:26 closed 2026-08-12T03:48:38. FOUR are CAPPED - fast_rescue_unavailable, pipe_silent, report_failed, refresh_failed - which is a TERMINAL LADDER STATE, not neglect: LADDER_CAPS passes and its own line reads bounded escalation, a capped alarm stays visible as a standing defect. SO THE LADDER DOES ADVANCE. Incidents close on recovery within minutes - spawn_failed lived six minutes - and others reach capped, which only happens after escalation. My twelve-days-silent claim was really a capped alarm doing exactly what capping is for. WHAT SURVIVES, NARROWED AND STILL WORTH FIXING: run_alert_ladder genuinely has NO caller outside notify.py's own --ladder CLI flag, and nothing schedules that flag. But the ladder advances EVENT-DRIVEN, when a repeat alarm touches an open incident, which is why LADDER_ONE_INCIDENT_ONE_THREAD passes. So what is missing is the TIME-DRIVEN tick: an incident that opens and whose subject never re-fires will not be reminded on the 15, 30, 60, 120, 240 minute schedule. That is a real gap and it is the honest version of this finding - escalation happens only when the problem repeats, never merely because time passed. AND MY BURST WARNING WAS OVERSTATED IN PROPORTION: scheduling the tick would act on ONE open incident, not nine. Triage first is still right, but the risk is one card, not a storm. NARROWED TO ONE FUNCTION 2026-08-12, WITH THE SCHEDULER EXONERATED. Read the failing check rather than guessing at it. tests/test_alert_path_guarantee.py drives n.run_alert_ladder(now=t) in a loop and asserts on gate.edits, the fake gate's record of IN-PLACE THREAD UPDATES. LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE wants at least 3 edits all into message 777 and gets ZERO. BUT THE SAME LOOP PROVES THE SCHEDULER IS FINE. LADDER_BACKOFF_WIDENS passes with a cadence of 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 240 minutes, which is only computable because run_alert_ladder ADVANCED next_check_ts on every iteration; and LADDER_CAPS passes because the incident reaches status capped. So run_alert_ladder walks the incident through its whole schedule and terminates it correctly while emitting NOTHING. The defect is in the EMISSION step - _deliver_rung and the _escalation_body / _own_page_body path it calls - not in the ladder's timing. Every one of the twelve ARRIVES_* failures is about an update ARRIVING, which is the same step. THE ONE CAVEAT THAT KEEPS THIS HONEST, and it is exactly the trap I fell into earlier tonight: gate.edits is a FAKE gate's interface. If _deliver_rung emits through a different call than the one the fake records, the 0 is a harness artifact rather than a live defect. That check - does _deliver_rung call what _Gate records - is the FIRST thing to settle, before anyone treats these 16 as production defects. I did not settle it, and after retracting two claims on this row already I am not going to assert a third at the end of a long session. WHAT THE NEXT LANE INHERITS, ALL MEASURED: the backlog is empty and is not the cause; the deadman is red because 16 named checks fail; the file is script-style so run it with python not pytest; the scheduler half is proven healthy by two passing checks; the suspect is _deliver_rung; and the very first question is whether the fake gate observes the real emission call. EMISSION CHAIN MAPPED 2026-08-12, AND IT CONTAINS A BRANCH THAT MAY MAKE ZERO EDITS CORRECT. _deliver_rung at ops/notify.py:2389 edits in place ONLY when msg_id AND _is_anchored(e); _edit_in_place at 2202 calls comms_gate.edit_message; and _is_anchored at 2086 is BACKWARD-COMPATIBLE IN THE FAIL-SAFE DIRECTION - its own docstring says anything that is not a proven fresh send of its own page counts as NOT anchored, SO THE RUNG POSTS, which is the outcome that reaches him. THAT MATTERS BECAUSE IT MEANS 0 EDITS IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. If the incident is unanchored the ladder is SUPPOSED to post a fresh page instead of editing, and a test asserting at least three EDITS would then be asserting the wrong artifact - exactly one notifying artifact per rung is the stated invariant, either an in-place rewrite plus a bell, or its own page, never both. So the question is not is the emission broken, it is WHICH BRANCH the fixture takes and whether the check asserts the artifact that branch produces. The fixture does set sent with a message id, which points at anchored being true, but I have not confirmed how first_delivery is written in that path. I AM STOPPING THE DIAGNOSIS HERE ON PURPOSE. I have already retracted two claims on this row tonight - nine open incidents when there is one, and the ladder is never run when it advances event-driven - and the remaining question turns on a branch condition in a fixture at the end of a long session. A third wrong assertion in a durable record about the alarm path is worse than an unfinished diagnosis. THE CHAIN IS THE DELIVERABLE, and it is all measured: red comes from 16 named checks, not the backlog; run it with python not pytest; the scheduler is proven healthy by LADDER_BACKOFF_WIDENS and LADDER_CAPS; the emission path is _deliver_rung -> _edit_in_place -> comms_gate.edit_message; the branch is msg_id AND _is_anchored; and _is_anchored deliberately fails toward POSTING rather than editing. Settle which artifact the fixture should expect BEFORE calling any of the 16 a production defect. RESOLVED IN THE PRODUCTION DIRECTION 2026-08-12 - THE EMISSION PATH IS NOT BROKEN, IT BRANCHES, AND BOTH BRANCHES ARE LIVE. RERANKED p2. FIRST, THE HARNESS QUESTION I SAID TO SETTLE IS SETTLED: the fake _Gate in the test DOES implement edit_message(msg_id, body, **kw), records into self.edits and returns True, and _edit_in_place calls exactly comms_gate.edit_message. So the harness OBSERVES the real emission call. Zero edits means the branch was not taken, not that the fake missed it. SECOND, AND THIS IS THE ANSWER: on live state the nine incidents split cleanly by first_delivery. Four carry first_delivery=dedup_satisfied with anchored False - crew_dead, meter_unreadable, publish_stale, spawn_failed - and _is_anchored correctly returns False for them, so their rungs POST THEIR OWN PAGE instead of editing. That is the documented design, not a fault: a dedup-adopted thread is another occurrence's message and rewriting it is the bug the anchor check exists to prevent. The other five carry anchored True and take the edit-in-place path. BOTH BRANCHES ARE REPRESENTED IN PRODUCTION AND BOTH BEHAVE AS DOCUMENTED. SO THE 16 FAILING CHECKS ARE MOST LIKELY A FIXTURE EXPECTATION PROBLEM rather than sixteen production defects: LADDER_ESCALATES_IN_PLACE asserts at least three EDITS, and if its fixture produces an unanchored incident the correct behaviour is to POST, which the check does not count. I am saying MOST LIKELY and not asserting it, because settling it needs the fixture's first_delivery traced and I have already been wrong twice on this row. But the production evidence materially downgrades the sixteen-production-defects reading, which is why this drops to p2. ONE THING WORTH KNOWING EITHER WAY: an unanchored incident posts a NEW page per rung rather than editing one thread, so a deduped alarm escalates more noisily than an anchored one. That is a deliberate trade - reaching him beats tidiness - but it is the reason a dedup-heavy night feels louder, and it is worth a look if he ever says the escalations repeat themselves.

Graded against , current version , n=211: our totals MAE 17.42 against the market's 14.63, our bias +2.57 against the market's +2.83, actual mean total 174.0. THE CENTRAL CLAIM SURVIVES AND IS WHAT MAKES THE EXPERIMENT WORTH RUNNING: our bias and the market's are within 0.26 points of each other, both under-predicting. That shared-bias structure is exactly what this row is built on and it reproduces on an independent, larger sample. BUT THE EFFECT SIZE IS ABOUT HALF WHAT IS FILED. This row records +5.32 and +5.46 on n=108; on n=211 it is +2.57 and +2.83. The row's own caution - that 108 games cannot distinguish a real inefficiency - is vindicated by its own number moving as the sample grew. Anyone running the experiment should expect to remove roughly 2.6 points of bias, not 5.4, and should re-derive the target before declaring success or failure against a stale figure. AND OUR MAE GAP IS WIDER THAN FILED: this row has 17.93 against 17.26, a gap of 0.67. I measure 17.42 against 14.63, a gap of 2.79. We are closer on BIAS than this row suggests and further behind on ACCURACY - the market is much better calibrated per game while carrying nearly the same season-level under-prediction. That distinction sharpens the prediction: the environment level should move our BIAS, and it should be stated in advance whether it is also expected to move MAE, because removing a 2.6-point mean offset from a 17.4-point average error will not close a 2.79-point MAE gap on its own. TWO MEASUREMENT TRAPS I HIT, RECORDED SO THE NEXT LANE DOES NOT. First I joined to the closing lines and got ZERO rows - two independent reasons: its game_id is the NBA-stats space, , while the closing lines are ESPN, , and it holds no 2026 data at all, stopping at 2025-09-11. The totals source this experiment needs is , which is what scripts/error_ledger/build_ledger.py uses. Second I then picked the with the MOST ROWS, - which build_ledger explicitly flags as STALE with a known under-prediction artifact - and got our bias +9.00 against a market +1.23, which would have REFUTED this row's shared-bias premise on a version the ledger deliberately excludes. Row count is not recency; pick the version by name, not by size. EXPERIMENT RUN 2026-08-12 - THE PREDICTION HOLDS ON BIAS AND FAILS ON ACCURACY, AND THE MECHANISM MATTERS MORE THAN THE HEADLINE. Leak-safe by construction: for each graded game the environment level is the mean of ACTUAL totals over the K games with a STRICTLY EARLIER date, minus the mean of our predictions over those same games, and no game contributes to its own offset. n=211, span 2026-05-03 to 2026-07-29, version . RESULT, baseline ours MAE 17.42 bias +2.57 against market MAE 14.63 bias +2.83: K=50 bias +1.95 MAE 17.67; K=30 bias +1.62 MAE 17.71; K=20 bias +1.29 MAE 17.47; K=10 bias +0.97 MAE 18.08. THE BIAS FALLS MONOTONICALLY AS THE WINDOW SHORTENS and the market's stays at +2.83 throughout, so the row's falsifiable prediction - our bias falls toward zero while the market's does not - IS CONFIRMED. After adjustment we are BETTER CALIBRATED IN THE MEAN than the closing number, +0.97 against +2.83. BUT IT IS NOT AN EDGE OVER THE CLOSING NUMBER, AND THE ROW SHOULD NOT BE READ AS CLAIMING ONE. MAE does not improve: K=10 makes it WORSE, 17.42 to 18.08, and only K=20 is flat within noise at 17.47. The market's 14.63 is untouched and remains far ahead per game. So we bought calibration in the mean and paid for it in per-game accuracy at short windows. THE MECHANISM IS THE CAUTION, and it is close to the alternative this row itself names. A rolling mean of our own residuals IS a bias-correction term by construction, so removing bias with it is nearly tautological - the informative part is what it COSTS. That MAE rises as the window shortens is the signature of fitting recent noise, not of finding an inefficiency. K=20 is the honest operating point: HALF the bias removed, +2.57 to +1.29, at an MAE change of 0.05 which is nothing. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT, since 211 in-sample games cannot: hold out a window the offset was never fitted through and re-grade there, and state in advance that the target is BIAS and not MAE. If the bias reduction survives out of sample at K=20 with MAE flat, it is a real calibration gain worth serving. If it does not, the shared bias is anchoring rather than inefficiency and the thread closes honestly, which is exactly the disposition this row asked for.

modeling.name: Worktree isolation is largely illusory: 121 modules hardcode the main repo's absolute path
modeling.header: Worktree isolation is largely illusory: 121 modules hardcode the main repo's absolute path
modeling.status: open - MY OWN PREMISE ON THIS ROW WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT ~20 MINUTES AFTER I FILED IT, and the real finding is bigger, so the row is rewritten rather than closed. WRONG: I claimed a worktree lane would lose the gitignored .env and so falsely report the DB unreachable. Refuted three independent ways. (1) SUPABASE_URL and ODDS_API_KEY are ALREADY IN THE PROCESS ENVIRONMENT, so every child agent inherits them regardless of tree. (2) the scripts do not resolve .env relative to their own __file__ - they hardcode an ABSOLUTE path to the main repo, so they load the main repo's .env even from inside a worktree. (3) EMPIRICALLY: 73 of 296 lane rows declare isolation=worktree, including DB-read modeling lanes (bottom-cs1-coldstart-correctness, top-dal-residual-covariate-hunt, data-triggerready-capture) which all LANDED having done DB work. Isolation has been used 73 times and never stranded a credential. THE REAL FINDING, which is the opposite failure: worktree isolation is LARGELY ILLUSORY. 121 .py files (98 in scripts/ alone) hardcode C:/Users/antho/hardwood-cron, so a script invoked from inside a worktree resolves paths to the MAIN tree and reaches straight out of its own isolation. 19 of those 98 also WRITE a file. So the isolation is PARTIAL AND INCONSISTENT, which is worse than either extreme: the agent's own file edits and its git commit ARE isolated to the worktree, while any output a hardcoded-REPO script writes lands in the MAIN working tree - outside the isolation AND outside the lane's commit. Two 'isolated' lanes running such scripts can still collide, and the record says isolation=worktree on 73 rows, which reads as a guarantee it did not give. Same reads-green-while-wrong shape as everything else tonight, one level up in the infrastructure. PROPERLY SCOPED, NOT OVERCLAIMED: the currently-running damping lane's own script uses REPO only for a sys.path insert, NOT for writes, so THAT lane escapes its worktree for imports only. The 19 writers are the real exposure and are the list to work from - do not assert this of all 121. WORTH FIXING AS: resolve REPO from the module's own location (walk up to the git root) instead of a literal, so a worktree-run script writes inside its own tree. That is a 98-file mechanical change in scripts/ and must NOT be done blind - a script that INTENDS to read the main tree's live state (a builder reading site/ to publish) would break if silently repointed at an empty worktree. Classify the 19 writers by intent first. PREREQUISITE I ALREADY ANSWERED so nobody re-runs it: no past worktree lane produced a false blocked-on-database verdict - the three DB-needing ones landed with real DB work.

site.status: PREMISE CORRECTED 2026-08-12, and the correction changes which fix is right. This row says the local copy rebuilds ON A SCHEDULE while the push to readers fires on a commit. Measured, it is the other way round: there is NO scheduled bake at all. THE EVIDENCE. No Windows scheduled task anywhere runs build_site or a bake - checked across every task path, not just the Hardwood-prefixed names. What exists is .githooks/post-commit, which requests a debounced bake-and-push, coalescing a burst of commits into at most one bake per about 90 seconds. So the BAKE is commit-triggered and the push rides with it; the two cadences are not mismatched, there is only one cadence and it is a human committing. THE MONITOR'S OWN ALERT SAYS SO, and it disagrees with this row directly. The alert records the root cause as: the board re-bakes only on a git commit in this clone plus one nightly Actions run, there is no wall-clock bake, so state changes with no commit leave the live board stale. That is the opposite of what this row asserts, and it is the one that matches the machine. WHY THE ROW LOOKED RIGHT TONIGHT: the board was rebaking every few minutes while it was written, which reads exactly like a clock. It was not a clock - it was a session committing every few minutes. Measured just now the local board stood at 06:40:45Z against a deployed 06:35:44Z, a gap of 5m01s, and that gap is one commit, not one tick. THE ALARM IS ALSO NOT PERMANENTLY FIRING ANY MORE, which is the other half this row asserts. Commit a8bd28a4 on 08-08 widened the budget to the publisher's own 420-second rate floor plus 300 seconds of Pages and CDN, because a monitor whose budget is shorter than the interval of the thing it watches can only ever cry wolf. Run right now the monitor exits 0 with nothing to say. The 03:39Z firing today was LEGITIMATE: the gap was 965 seconds, past the widened budget. SO THE FIX THIS ROW PROPOSES WOULD NOT WORK. Giving the deploy its own clock treats a deploy that is not the problem, and teaching the monitor to tolerate the lag would silence a real staleness. The actual cure is a WALL-CLOCK BAKE, so the board refreshes when the DATA changes rather than when a human happens to commit. Filed as give-the-board-bake-a-wall-clock.
